newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Asia's new boom town is APEC summit venue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asia's new boom town is APEC summit venue.

text.p: Next week's APEC summit in Subic Bay is about to prove wrong the sceptics who four years said the freeport's slogan of "Aim High" was an advice to Filipino men urinating against the town's walls.

On November 25, Subic will host the fourth annual summit of Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum leaders in an event that will showcase its rise as one of Asia's fastest growing business centres.
Subic used to be the United States' biggest overseas naval base until 1992 when the Philippine Senate refused to renew the lease.
The closure of the Subic Naval Base and Clark, a nearby U.S. air base, put nearly 50,000 people out of jobs and starved hundreds of bars and night spots of dollar-rich customers.
"We said to people, 'Look we have no budget but if you work now, you may soon get jobs'," said Richard Gordon, chairman of the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority.
The workers, who had learnt their skills maintaining American warships, agreed and went to work as volunteers.
"Pretty soon, people were working power plants, cutting the grass and making sure there was no pillaging," said Gordon.

The initial stability provided by Gordon and his volunteer band convinced dozens of foreign companies that Subic, converted into a freeport after the departure of the Americans, was the right place to invest in.

With its few remaining missile silos and large sheds, Subic still has the feel of a garrison but it now boasts of being home to 220 companies, and government officials say promises of investment amount to over $1 billion.
"From a bastion of security to a bastion of economic prosperity," said one recent hoarding.
Slogans like this one and "Aim High" are common under the leadership of Gordon who has taken up Subic's cause with a missionary zeal.
Among Subic's biggest investors are Taiwanese computer giant Acer Inc, power firm Enron and courier company Federal Express.
The freeport employing 35,000 people makes products that include computer boards, telephones, CD Roms, clothes, diving suits, tape recorders and even armoured personnel carriers.

Gordon said Subic Bay would now exploit its tourism potential. Endowed with 12 hectares (30 acres) of thick rainforest where American marines used to learn jungle survival skills from the indigenous Aeta tribesmen, Subic could be the ideal haunt for ecological tourism, he said.
The former baseland, where the freeport is located, covers 18 hectares (44 acres) but including the surrounding municipalities, Subic extends over 53,000 hectares (130,000 acres).
The Philippines has said Subic offers an attractive alternative to Hong Kong for businesses which may want to move out after the British colony returns to Chinese control next year.
"We are three and half hours away from Asian indigenous communities and at the gateway to the Asia Pacific," said Gordon.

Located about 80 km (50 miles) north of Manila, Subic used to be a Spanish naval base until 1898 when the Americans took it over and stayed on until 1992, except for a brief period during World War Two when Japanese forces occupied it.

Its fortifications made it the ideal location for APEC leaders from the point of security, an overriding concern for the Philippines as the guest list includes "high-risk" heads of government like U.S. President Bill Clinton.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, South Korea, and the United States of America.

The security ring thrown around Subic in preparation for the arrival of the leaders has invited the wrath of human rights groups and some local newspapers who said restrictions imposed on peoples' movements were reminiscent of martial law days.
But Gordon firmly rejected the accusations saying: "Baloney."
